easterEgg.heading: You found the Klingon translation!
easterEgg.intro: This interface has been translated into tlhIngan Hol as a tribute to Star Trek and its fans. Here are some of our favourite translations:
easterEgg.brandNameMeaning: War Game Academy — because to a Klingon, all games are battle training
easterEgg.taglineLabel: Where screen time becomes quality time
easterEgg.privacyMeaning: So’wI’ is a cloaking device — what a Klingon calls keeping something out of sight
easterEgg.termsMeaning: The pact is the agreement itself, sworn to before the first battle
easterEgg.honorMeaning: A warrior who preys on the weak has no honour to speak of
easterEgg.retiredNote: Those last three names are retired. The Privacy Policy, the Terms & Conditions and the Anti-Bullying Policy now read the same in every locale, Federation Standard included — they are binding documents, and no family should have to decode their own rights. An honourable translation, but the wrong battlefield for one.
easterEgg.note: Date and time formatting appears in English because the browser’s Intl APIs don’t have Klingon locale data. Klingons don’t use a 7-day week anyway.

whoLeads.question: Who leads the sessions, and how are Gedus vetted?
whoLeads.answer: Every session is hosted by a Gedu — a Game Educator who’s also a gamer and knows how to support children in-game and out. Registering as a Gedu does not put someone in front of children: before an admin certifies a Gedu, they present a criminal record extract for working with children — the Finnish rikosrekisteriote, which they order themselves from the Legal Register Centre and which must be less than six months old when they show it to us — and they read and accept the contract they work under. We keep no copy of the extract and record nothing out of it, only that an acceptable one was shown and when. Until an admin has certified their account, a Gedu cannot be assigned to a club or camp, cannot start a voice room, and cannot email a session report to families.

safety.question: Can strangers talk to my child, and is anything recorded?
safety.answer: No — a club’s voice room is not a public room anyone can find. It exists only during that group’s session window, opening five minutes before the session starts and closing five minutes after it ends, and the only people who can enter are the members of that group, the Game Educator assigned to it, and School of Gaming admins; that check runs on our server every time someone joins, so a child with no place in that group has no way in. There is no direct-message feature anywhere on the platform: text chat during a call goes to the whole room, lives only as long as the call does, and is never stored. Nothing in the app records, transcribes or stores a session — there is no recording feature to switch on and nowhere for a recording to go. Only the Gedu and admins hold the moderator controls: muting a microphone, locking one, and moving someone to a separate space. In-game chat is a separate thing, run by the games themselves — on School of Gaming’s own Minecraft server our Gedus can mute, kick and ban a player.

howToStart.question: chay’ jIQaplaH?
howToStart.answer: Create a parent account, add your child as a gamer from My SOG, then browse the shop and enrol them — the signup panel asks who the seat is for, and prompts you to add a gamer if you have not yet. Once you have signed up we place your child in a group with a Gedu before their first session, and the club then appears on My SOG for both of you. They join sessions through your account — you switch to their profile — so they never need a password of their own.

isItASchool.question: Is this school?
isItASchool.answer: No. Gaming is a hobby like any other, and that is how we run it: a Game Educator is there to guide and help, not to grade. Nothing in Sogverse gives a child a mark, sets homework or holds an exam. What your child does get is a group of their own, a Gedu who knows them, and a written report after each session so you can see what they worked on and how it went.

ages.question: What ages is this for?
ages.answer: Every club, camp and event carries its own age range, shown on its page and on its card in the shop — and the shop filters by age band, so you can see only what fits your child. Across the platform those ranges run from age 7 to 17. The games themselves have their own ratings, and we follow Finland’s official age-rating guidance: a child may play a game rated up to three years above their own age when a parent is present and comfortable with it, and never a game rated 18+. Signing your child up confirms you are happy with the ratings of the games involved.

games.question: Which games do you run, and does my child need to own the game?
games.answer: Our clubs, camps and events run in Minecraft (Java, Bedrock and Education editions), Roblox Studio, Fortnite, Rocket League and Pokémon GO, alongside sessions on esports, programming, AI and game creation — every club, camp and event page names the game it is built around and says plainly what you need. Fortnite, Rocket League, Pokémon GO and Roblox Studio are free to download; your child needs a free account for them. Minecraft Java and Minecraft Bedrock are paid games your family buys once from the publisher — the price is not included in ours, and the edition matters, so the page tells you which one and where to get it. For Minecraft Education there is nothing to buy and no school account to arrange: School of Gaming provides the accounts used in the session, and your child only downloads the game itself, free of charge.

equipment.question: What equipment does my child need?
equipment.answer: It depends on the game, and every club, camp and event says so on its own page. Minecraft Java needs a computer — Windows, Mac or Linux — and the console, phone and tablet edition will not work. Roblox Studio runs on Windows PCs and Macs only: not on a tablet, Chromebook, phone or console. Minecraft Bedrock runs on consoles, phones, tablets and Windows PCs, and Rocket League on Windows PCs, PlayStation, Xbox and Nintendo Switch. Pokémon GO needs a phone or tablet with GPS and a mobile data connection, because it is played outdoors. Online sessions themselves run in the browser, over voice, so your child also needs a microphone — the session screen has a microphone picker and a live test bar so they can check it is the right one before they speak.

billing.question: What does it cost, and how does billing work?
billing.answer: Prices are set per club, camp and event, and each one shows its own price on its page, in euros and including VAT. How you pay depends on what you are signing up for: a club is a monthly subscription, billed every month with no fixed commitment; a camp or an event is a single payment made once at signup, with nothing further to pay; and a municipality club is paid for by the municipality, so there is nothing to pay us. Each child’s place in each club is its own monthly subscription, named after the child and the club, so a family with two children in two clubs sees four lines — all on the same card. If you sign up before a club has started, nothing is charged that day: the page tells you the date of your first payment before you commit. Your saved cards, invoices and subscriptions all live in the Payment & billing card on My SOG, which opens Stripe’s own secure billing page.

cancellation.question: Can I cancel, and what is your refund policy?
cancellation.answer: A club runs as a monthly subscription with no fixed commitment, and you can cancel whenever you like, at no cost, from the Payment & billing card on My SOG, which opens Stripe’s secure billing page. Your child keeps their place until the end of the billing period you have already paid for — their club page shows the date of their last session while the membership winds down. Every club also carries a 30-day money-back guarantee: if it turns out not to be right for your child, email {supportEmail} within 30 days of their first session and we refund everything you have paid towards that club — there is no form and no reason to give. Camps are booked and paid as a one-off, so they work differently: cancel 14 days or more before the camp starts and you get a full refund; between 7 and 14 days before, we refund you minus a €50 administration fee; less than 7 days before we cannot refund the payment, because the place has been held and prepared for your child — unless it is a medical emergency or something genuinely outside your control. If your child cannot attend because of illness, send us a doctor’s certificate at {supportEmail} and we refund you.

severalChildren.question: I have several children — how do accounts and payments work?
severalChildren.answer: You hold one parent account, and you create a gamer account for each child from My SOG — first name, birth month and year, and optionally gender. A child never creates an account of their own, and your account can hold up to seven gamers. Payments stay on your card: each child’s place in each club is its own line, so you can see and cancel them one at a time, but they all sit on one payment method and one invoice history, which you reach from the Payment & billing card on My SOG. There is no per-family bundle to buy and no separate account to set up per child.

languages.question: What language are sessions run in?
languages.answer: Two different settings, and they do not have to match. Every club, camp and event is delivered in one language — Finnish, Swedish, English or French — shown on its page and usable as a filter in the shop. Separately, the language you read Sogverse in is your own choice, from the picker in the site header. Changing it changes the app, not the language your child’s sessions are run in, so a Finnish-speaking parent can read the site in Finnish and enrol their child in an English club.

municipalityClubs.question: What is a municipality club, and how do we join one?
municipalityClubs.answer: A municipality club is a club we run together with a Finnish municipality. Depending on the municipality it meets either online from home or in person at your child’s school, and a professional Game Educator is there to guide it either way. The municipality pays for it, so there is nothing to pay us when you register — some municipalities charge families a small fee of their own, which they will tell you about. You do not need a code or a referral: search for your municipality on our municipality clubs page, and if we have reached it, its clubs are listed there and you register your child directly, with no payment step. Places are limited and clubs often have a waiting list, so if your child stops attending, please tell us so the place can be offered to the next gamer. We also run clubs that are open to everyone, which a gamer can join wherever they live.

gamerAccounts.question: How does my child sign in, and what is the parent PIN?
gamerAccounts.answer: Your child has no login of their own. A gamer account carries an internal Sogverse address rather than your child’s real email address, it is linked to your parent account, and your child enters Sogverse by switching to their profile from yours — there is no password for them to lose or share. Getting into the parent side takes a four-digit PIN that only you know, so a password saved in the browser is not enough to buy anything or change a child’s account, and the session locks again the moment you switch to a child’s profile or sign out. If you forget the PIN, we email a reset link to the address on your account and nowhere else — a child pressing “Forgot your PIN?” simply sends you an email.

childData.question: What do you store about my child?
childData.answer: Their first name, their birth month and year — we do not ask for the day — and optionally their gender, plus your family surname, because your child is part of your family; a Gedu’s roster and the voice room show your child’s first name only. Their account carries an internal Sogverse address rather than a real email address, and optionally we hold their username in the games their clubs use — today Minecraft and Roblox — and the id that game gives them, so we can recognise them in a session. There is no photo: the picture beside their name is a pattern generated from their account id. Alongside that we keep what running a club requires — which clubs, camps and events they are signed up for, their attendance, and the session reports and short staff notes their Gedus write. To see, correct or delete anything we hold about your child, email {supportEmail}. We keep your information for as long as you have an account and delete or anonymise it if you close one, except where the law requires us to keep certain records longer, as Finnish accounting law does for payment records.

becomeGedu.question: How do I become a Game Educator?
becomeGedu.answer: Register for a Gedu account on our Game Educator sign-up page: it asks for your name and email, a password, and optionally your phone number, the languages you speak, the areas you can work in on site, and your Minecraft or Roblox username. You can sign in straight away. Before an admin certifies your account two things happen: you read and accept the contract you would work under, and you present a criminal record extract for working with children (rikosrekisteriote), which you order yourself from the Legal Register Centre and which must be less than six months old — we keep no copy of it. Certification is what opens the rest: until then you cannot be assigned to a club or camp, cannot start a voice room, and cannot reset Minecraft Education passwords.

joiningSession.question: How do I join my session when it starts?
joiningSession.answer: Open My SOG and find your club. Five minutes before your session starts, the button on it changes from a locked “Opens…” to Join voice room — tap that and you are in. There is nothing to install and no code to type, and until then the button tells you the day and time it opens. If it says “Matching with a Gedu” instead, you are signed up but we have not put you in a group yet; that happens before your first session, and your Gedu will be there when it does.

micTrouble.question: Nobody can hear me, or I cannot hear anyone — what do I check?
micTrouble.answer: Tap the small arrow next to the microphone button. It opens your microphone settings: pick the right microphone from the list, then talk — the bar moves when your microphone is working, and if it does not move, something else has the microphone. Then three things to check. Is your microphone button red? That means you are muted, so tap it to unmute. Does it show a padlock? Your Gedu has locked it for a moment, and they will unlock it. And if a red message says we cannot reach your microphone, close any other app or tab using it, allow microphone access in your browser’s settings, and tap Reload. If you cannot hear anyone, check the volume on your computer and that your headphones are plugged in properly. Still stuck? Tell your Gedu in the session — they can help.

someoneIsMean.question: What if someone is mean to me in a session?
someoneIsMean.answer: Tell your Gedu. Say it out loud in the session, or tell them afterwards — they are there for exactly this, and it is never telling tales. You can also tell a parent, and they can email us. Your Gedu will talk with the person about what happened and help them put it right. If it keeps happening they take firmer steps: a quiet one-to-one chat, muting someone or limiting what they can do in the game, asking them to sit out the rest of the session, and — if nothing changes — time away from our clubs altogether. Being unkind is never something you have to put up with here.

certification.question: What does certification mean, and what can I not do until then?
certification.answer: Certification is an admin confirming your account is ready to work with children. Two things come before it: accepting your Gedu contract, and presenting a criminal record extract for working with children (rikosrekisteriote) that is less than six months old. You order the extract yourself from the Legal Register Centre. We keep no copy of it and record nothing out of it — only that an acceptable one was shown, and when. Both show their status in your settings. Until you are certified you cannot be assigned to a group, and your Tools section stays closed: you cannot start an instant voice room, and you cannot reset Minecraft Education passwords. You also cannot email a session report to families or add photos to one. Everything else is open now: signing in, My SOG, your profile and coverage areas, and reading and accepting the contract. Help & feedback is here whether or not you are certified — use the form above if you are waiting and want to know where you stand.

groupAssignment.question: How do I get assigned to a group?
groupAssignment.answer: An admin assigns you. Assignments are made from a club, camp or event’s groups panel on the admin side — you cannot assign yourself, and there is no request to submit — and you can hold one group per club, camp or event. Two things decide whether you appear as an option: your account has to be certified, and the admin picking a Gedu can filter by the languages you speak and see the areas you have said you can work in, so keeping your spoken languages and coverage areas up to date in your settings is what puts you in front of the right groups. There is no email when an assignment is made — the group appears on your My SOG, with its next session, the next time you open it.

safeguardingConcern.question: I have a safeguarding concern mid-session — what do I do?
safeguardingConcern.answer: Deal with the immediate situation in the room first — you hold the moderator controls: mute a microphone, lock it, move someone into a private space away from the group, or end the session. Then put it on record the same day, while it is fresh. Every session has a staff note, marked for Gedus and admins, that families never see; it is where an incident, bullying or a worry about a gamer belongs. There is also a per-gamer note on the group roster that stays with that child in that group, session to session, and is likewise Gedu- and admin-only. Neither is visible to any family. A note is a record, not an alert: nobody is paged by it, so anything urgent, or anything that needs someone beyond the group, goes to the office at {supportEmail} as well.

gamerCannotConnect.question: A gamer cannot connect and the session has started — what can I do?
gamerCannotConnect.answer: Two things you can do inside the product, and one you cannot. Check who is actually in the room against your roster — the participant list only shows people who are connected right now, so a name missing from it is a gamer who has not made it in, and nothing marks that for you; you read it off the list. To reach the family, open the group’s roster in the group workspace: each row carries the family’s contact email, which you copy with a tap, and there is a copy-all control above the list. You send from your own mail — there is no in-app message to a family, no text message, and no phone number on the roster. What you cannot do is admit them yourself: entry is decided by our server on the gamer’s own request, and they need an active place in that group with the session window open. If they hold a place and still cannot get in, the fastest fix is usually on their side — allow the browser microphone access, close whatever else is using it, reload. If it is something we need to fix, mail the office at {supportEmail}.

parentPin.question: What is the parent PIN, and what if I forget it?
parentPin.answer: Your parent PIN is a four-digit code you set the first time you use your parent account. It gates the parent side of Sogverse rather than each separate action: you unlock once, and the session locks again the moment you switch to a gamer profile or sign out — so a password saved in the browser is not enough on its own to buy anything or change a child’s account. If you forget it, tap “Forgot your PIN?” on the PIN screen: we email a reset link to the address on your account and nowhere else, so a child pressing it simply sends you an email. The link lasts 24 hours and works once. You can also change a PIN you still know from Settings.

sessionReports.question: Will I hear how sessions went?
sessionReports.answer: Yes. After a session your child’s Game Educator writes a report on it — what the group worked on, how it went, and the moments worth remembering — often with photos. It appears on that club, camp or event’s page in My SOG, under Sessions, alongside every earlier report and the sessions still to come, and your child sees the same reports in their own My SOG. When the Gedu sends the report, it also arrives by email, addressed to you alone — every family receives their own separate email and no family sees another. You will also see your own child’s attendance mark for each session on that page; your child does not see attendance, and no family ever sees another child’s.

missedSessions.question: What if we miss a session, or join a club partway through?
missedSessions.answer: A club stays open for new gamers while it is running, so you can join partway through a term — the club page shows what is on next and how many seats are left. Camps and events are different: a camp closes to new sign-ups on the day it starts, because the group starts together, and an event closes once its session has ended. A club is billed as a full month from the day you sign up, so joining mid-month does not reduce that month’s payment; if a club has not started yet, nothing is charged on the day you sign up and the page tells you the date of your first payment. If your child misses a single session there is nothing to do — their place is not affected. Their Gedu marks attendance for each session and you will see that mark on the club page. A session missed is not made up or refunded; on a municipality club, repeated unexcused absences may open the place for the next family on the waiting list, which you agree to when you register.

sessionTimes.question: What time do sessions happen in our timezone?
sessionTimes.answer: In yours. Session times are authored in Finnish time and shown to you converted to your own device’s timezone automatically, everywhere they appear — on a club’s page, on its card, and on your My SOG. When your timezone differs from the club’s, the time carries a short timezone marker beside it so the conversion is visible; when you are in the same zone as the club, there is nothing to convert and no marker. Because the conversion is real, a club running on two Finnish weekdays can land on different weekdays for you, and the schedule you see is grouped by your weekdays, not ours. A camp’s start and end dates are plain calendar dates and do not shift.
